You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
The failing test `testRoundTripNames()` calls `checkName()` with various string inputs, including a string with characters outside the ASCII range (line 126). The current bug report states that `TarUtils.parseName` does not properly handle characters outside the 0-127 range, resulting in incorrect names when parsing tar entries with special characters.

Inspecting the implementation of `TarUtils.parseName(byte[] buffer, int offset, int length)`, the method initializes a `StringBuffer`, then iterates over the byte array from offset to offset+length. It appends characters by casting each byte directly to `char`, i.e., `result.append((char) buffer[i]);`. This approach is problematic because it treats signed bytes as unsigned chars without proper encoding consideration, which leads to incorrect characters for bytes > 127.

The current report suggests fixing the issue by converting each byte to a one-byte array and then creating a new `String` from that single byte (using platform default or appropriate encoding). This method preserves the exact byte values instead of interpreting them as signed chars, which avoids the character corruption.

The root cause is that `parseName` does not properly handle non-ASCII bytes due to direct `(char)` casting of bytes. This explains why the special characters become corrupted.

The test fails because the name parsed from bytes does not match the original string containing special characters (like "±"), validating the report's observation.

Recent bug reports about ZIP handling or trailing spaces in octal size fields are unrelated to this character encoding issue and can be ignored.

# Diagnosis

`TarUtils.parseName` incorrectly converts bytes to `char` by casting `(char) buffer[i]`, which mishandles bytes with values > 127, causing corrupted names for tar entries with non-ASCII characters. The proper fix is to decode bytes individually using a `new String(byte[], encoding)` approach or equivalent to preserve byte values correctly.

# Next step

The fix should be applied in the `TarUtils.parseName` method.
Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test `testRoundTripNames` reveals a problem with handling special characters in tar entry names. The cause lies in the `TarUtils.parseName` method, which converts bytes to characters by directly casting `(char) buffer[i]`. This incorrect treatment of bytes as chars mishandles bytes outside the 0-127 ASCII range, corrupting names with special characters. The bug report highlights the issue and suggests using a new String created from single-byte arrays to preserve byte values correctly. Recent similar issues are unrelated to this character encoding problem. Thus, the root cause is the direct casting of bytes to chars in `parseName` without proper character decoding, leading to incorrect names for tar entries with non-ASCII characters.

Suggested fix location:
TarUtils.parseName(byte[], int, int)

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
